$comment: SQL playground challenges. Edit freely, then run `npm run sql:expected` to regenerate each `expected` from its `solution`.

challenges.title: Employees and their departments
challenges.description: List every employee who belongs to a department, with the department name. Return `name` and `department`.
hints: Join `employees` to `departments` on `employees.department_id = departments.id`.
An INNER JOIN drops the employee with no department - that is what is wanted here.
challenges.solution:
SELECT e.name, d.name AS department
FROM employees e
JOIN departments d ON d.id = e.department_id

challenges.title: Departments with nobody in them
challenges.description: Find the departments that have no employees. Return `name`.
hints: Start from `departments` and LEFT JOIN `employees`.
Rows with no match have NULL employee columns - filter on that. NOT EXISTS works too.
challenges.solution:
SELECT d.name
FROM departments d
LEFT JOIN employees e ON e.department_id = d.id
WHERE e.id IS NULL

challenges.title: Who reports to whom
challenges.description: List each employee with their manager's name. The CEO has no manager and should still appear, with a NULL manager. Return `employee` and `manager`.
hints: This is a self join: `employees` joined to `employees` again under another alias.
Use a LEFT JOIN so the person with no manager is kept.
challenges.solution:
SELECT e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN employees m ON m.id = e.manager_id

challenges.title: Customers who never ordered
challenges.description: Find customers who have never placed an order. Return `name`.
hints: An anti-join: LEFT JOIN `orders` and keep rows where the order is NULL.
Or: `WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id)`.
challenges.solution:
SELECT c.name
FROM customers c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id)

challenges.title: Value of each delivered order
challenges.description: For every **delivered** order, return the order `id`, the customer `name` and the order `total` (sum of quantity x unit_price over its lines), largest total first (ties by order id).
hints: Three tables: `orders`, `customers` and `order_items`.
GROUP BY the order, then ORDER BY the total descending.
challenges.solution:
SELECT o.id, c.name, SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price) AS total
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
WHERE o.status = 'delivered'
GROUP BY o.id, c.name
ORDER BY total DESC, o.id

challenges.title: Headcount per department
challenges.description: How many employees does each department have? Include departments with nobody (count 0). Return `department` and `headcount`, biggest first, then by name.
hints: LEFT JOIN from `departments` so empty ones survive.
COUNT(e.id) counts only matched employees; COUNT(*) would count 1 for an empty department.
challenges.solution:
SELECT d.name AS department, COUNT(e.id) AS headcount
FROM departments d
LEFT JOIN employees e ON e.department_id = d.id
GROUP BY d.id, d.name
ORDER BY headcount DESC, department

challenges.title: Departments with a high average salary
challenges.description: Which departments have an average salary above 100,000? Return `department` and `avg_salary` rounded to the nearest whole number.
hints: Filtering on an aggregate needs HAVING, not WHERE.
ROUND(AVG(salary)) gives a whole number.
challenges.solution:
SELECT d.name AS department, ROUND(AVG(e.salary)) AS avg_salary
FROM employees e
JOIN departments d ON d.id = e.department_id
GROUP BY d.name
HAVING AVG(e.salary) > 100000

challenges.title: Revenue by product category
challenges.description: Total revenue per product category from orders that were **not cancelled**. Return `category` and `revenue`.
hints: Revenue is quantity x unit_price from `order_items` (the price actually charged), not `products.price`.
Join `order_items` to `orders` to exclude cancelled ones, and to `products` for the category.
challenges.solution:
SELECT p.category, SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price) AS revenue
FROM order_items i
JOIN orders o ON o.id = i.order_id
JOIN products p ON p.id = i.product_id
WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled'
GROUP BY p.category

challenges.title: Customers with more than three orders
challenges.description: Which customers have placed more than three orders (any status)? Return `name` and `orders`.
hints: GROUP BY customer and COUNT the orders.
HAVING COUNT(*) > 3.
challenges.solution:
SELECT c.name, COUNT(*) AS orders
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
GROUP BY c.id, c.name
HAVING COUNT(*) > 3

challenges.title: HTTP status code counts
challenges.description: Count the requests in `web_logs` by HTTP status code. Return `status` and `requests`, most common first (ties by status).
hints: GROUP BY status.
ORDER BY the count descending - and break ties by status so the order is stable.
challenges.solution:
SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS requests
FROM web_logs
GROUP BY status
ORDER BY requests DESC, status

challenges.title: Slow endpoints
challenges.description: Find paths whose average `response_ms` is over 300 ms, counting only paths with at least 20 requests. Return `path`, `requests` and `avg_ms` (rounded to a whole number), slowest first.
hints: Both conditions are on aggregates, so both go in HAVING.
ROUND(AVG(response_ms)).
challenges.solution:
SELECT path, COUNT(*) AS requests, ROUND(AVG(response_ms)) AS avg_ms
FROM web_logs
GROUP BY path
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 20 AND AVG(response_ms) > 300
ORDER BY avg_ms DESC

challenges.title: Salary rank within each department
challenges.description: Rank employees by salary within their department, highest first, using RANK() so ties share a rank. Skip employees with no department. Return `department`, `name`, `salary` and `salary_rank`, ordered by department, then rank, then name.
hints: `RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY salary DESC)`.
Two Senior Engineers earn the same - RANK gives both the same number and skips the next.
challenges.solution:
SELECT d.name AS department, e.name, e.salary,
       RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY e.department_id ORDER BY e.salary DESC) AS salary_rank
FROM employees e
JOIN departments d ON d.id = e.department_id
ORDER BY department, salary_rank, e.name

challenges.title: Top earner in each department
challenges.description: Return the single highest-paid employee in each department (if two tie, the one hired first). Return `department`, `name` and `salary`.
hints: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary DESC, hire_date) numbers each department's rows from 1.
Window functions cannot go in WHERE: compute them in a CTE or subquery, then filter `= 1` outside.
challenges.solution:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT e.*, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary DESC, hire_date) AS rn
  FROM employees e
  WHERE department_id IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT d.name AS department, r.name, r.salary
FROM ranked r
JOIN departments d ON d.id = r.department_id
WHERE r.rn = 1

challenges.title: Days between a customer's orders
challenges.description: For each order, show how many days have passed since the same customer's previous order (NULL for their first). Return `customer_id`, `order_date` and `days_since_previous`, ordered by customer then date.
hints: LAG(order_date) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date) gives the previous order's date.
SQLite stores dates as text: `julianday(a) - julianday(b)` gives the difference in days.
challenges.solution:
SELECT customer_id, order_date,
       CAST(julianday(order_date) - julianday(LAG(order_date) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY order_date)) AS INTEGER) AS days_since_previous
FROM orders
ORDER BY customer_id, order_date

challenges.title: Running total of revenue
challenges.description: For each day with non-cancelled orders, show that day's revenue and the running total so far. Return `order_date`, `revenue` and `running_total`, in date order.
hints: First aggregate revenue per day (a CTE helps).
Then `SUM(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY order_date)` accumulates it.
challenges.solution:
WITH daily AS (
  SELECT o.order_date, SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price) AS revenue
  FROM orders o
  JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
  WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled'
  GROUP BY o.order_date
)
SELECT order_date, revenue, SUM(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY order_date) AS running_total
FROM daily
ORDER BY order_date

challenges.title: Salary against the department average
challenges.description: Show each employee who has a department, their salary, their department's average salary (rounded) and the difference (salary minus that rounded average). Return `name`, `salary`, `dept_avg` and `difference`.
hints: `AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY department_id)` keeps every row, unlike GROUP BY.
Compute the rounded average once in a subquery or CTE, then subtract.
challenges.solution:
WITH withavg AS (
  SELECT name, salary, ROUND(AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY department_id)) AS dept_avg
  FROM employees
  WHERE department_id IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT name, salary, dept_avg, salary - dept_avg AS difference
FROM withavg

challenges.title: Customers who spend more than average
challenges.description: Considering only non-cancelled orders, find customers whose total spend is above the average total spend per customer (among customers who bought something). Return `name` and `spend`.
hints: CTE 1: total spend per customer.
Then compare each total with `(SELECT AVG(spend) FROM that_cte)`.
challenges.solution:
WITH spend AS (
  SELECT o.customer_id, SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price) AS spend
  FROM orders o
  JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
  WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled'
  GROUP BY o.customer_id
)
SELECT c.name, s.spend
FROM spend s
JOIN customers c ON c.id = s.customer_id
WHERE s.spend > (SELECT AVG(spend) FROM spend)

challenges.title: Month-over-month revenue change
challenges.description: Revenue per month (non-cancelled orders) with the change from the previous month. Return `month` (YYYY-MM), `revenue` and `change` (NULL for the first month), in month order.
hints: `strftime('%Y-%m', order_date)` gives the month.
Aggregate by month in a CTE, then `revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month)`.
challenges.solution:
WITH monthly AS (
  SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', o.order_date) AS month, SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price) AS revenue
  FROM orders o
  JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id
  WHERE o.status <> 'cancelled'
  GROUP BY month
)
SELECT month, revenue, revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS change
FROM monthly
ORDER BY month

challenges.title: Org chart levels
challenges.description: Using a recursive CTE, give every employee their level in the org chart: the CEO is level 1, their direct reports level 2, and so on. Return `name` and `level`, ordered by level then name.
hints: Anchor: the employee whose `manager_id IS NULL`, at level 1.
Recursive step: join `employees` to the CTE on `employees.manager_id = cte.id`, with `level + 1`.
challenges.solution:
WITH RECURSIVE chart(id, name, level) AS (
  SELECT id, name, 1 FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.id, e.name, c.level + 1
  FROM employees e
  JOIN chart c ON e.manager_id = c.id
)
SELECT name, level
FROM chart
ORDER BY level, name

challenges.title: Orders on every day of a week
challenges.description: For each day from 2025-07-01 to 2025-07-07, show how many orders were placed - including days with none. Return `day` and `orders`, in date order.
hints: There is no calendar table: generate the seven dates with a recursive CTE using `date(day, '+1 day')`.
LEFT JOIN `orders` to the dates and COUNT(o.id).
challenges.solution:
WITH RECURSIVE days(day) AS (
  SELECT '2025-07-01'
  UNION ALL
  SELECT date(day, '+1 day') FROM days WHERE day < '2025-07-07'
)
SELECT d.day, COUNT(o.id) AS orders
FROM days d
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.order_date = d.day
GROUP BY d.day
ORDER BY d.day

challenges.title: Second highest salary
challenges.description: The classic: return the second highest **distinct** salary in the company, as a single column `salary`.
hints: Distinct matters: two people tied for a salary still count as one value.
`SELECT DISTINCT salary ... ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1`, or `MAX(salary) WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) ...)`.
challenges.solution:
SELECT MAX(salary) AS salary
FROM employees
WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees)

challenges.title: Duplicate email addresses
challenges.description: Find email addresses used by more than one customer. Return `email` and `uses`.
hints: GROUP BY email.
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1.
challenges.solution:
SELECT email, COUNT(*) AS uses
FROM customers
GROUP BY email
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1

challenges.title: Employees who earn more than their manager
challenges.description: Find employees whose salary is higher than their own manager's. Return `employee`, `salary`, `manager` and `manager_salary`.
hints: Self join `employees` as e and m on `e.manager_id = m.id`.
Then `WHERE e.salary > m.salary`.
challenges.solution:
SELECT e.name AS employee, e.salary, m.name AS manager, m.salary AS manager_salary
FROM employees e
JOIN employees m ON m.id = e.manager_id
WHERE e.salary > m.salary

challenges.title: De-duplicate customers
challenges.description: Customers sharing an email are duplicates. Return the `id` and `name` of the customers to **keep**: for each email, only the one who signed up first.
hints: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY email ORDER BY signup_date) is 1 for the earliest signup of each email.
Keep the rows where it is 1. In a real clean-up you would DELETE the others.
challenges.solution:
WITH numbered AS (
  SELECT id, name, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY email ORDER BY signup_date, id) AS rn
  FROM customers
)
SELECT id, name FROM numbered WHERE rn = 1

challenges.title: Top clients by error responses
challenges.description: Which three IP addresses received the most error responses (status 400 and above)? Return `ip` and `errors`, most first (ties by ip).
hints: Filter rows with WHERE status >= 400 before grouping.
ORDER BY errors DESC LIMIT 3.
challenges.solution:
SELECT ip, COUNT(*) AS errors
FROM web_logs
WHERE status >= 400
GROUP BY ip
ORDER BY errors DESC, ip
LIMIT 3

challenges.title: Hourly error rate
challenges.description: For each hour of the day (00-23, across all three days), return the number of requests and the percentage that were server errors (status 500+), rounded to one decimal place. Return `hour`, `requests` and `error_pct`, in hour order.
hints: `strftime('%H', ts)` extracts the hour.
`SUM(CASE WHEN status >= 500 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)` counts errors; multiply by 100.0 before dividing so the division is not integer division.
challenges.solution:
SELECT strftime('%H', ts) AS hour,
       COUNT(*) AS requests,
       ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN status >= 500 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*), 1) AS error_pct
FROM web_logs
GROUP BY hour
ORDER BY hour
